1.pericope_label: Abram comes up out of Egypt very rich, and returns to the altar at Bethel

schools.summary: Build on the word for rich meaning heavy, and enumerate the burdens of wealth — care in getting, fear in keeping, temptation in using, guilt in abusing, sorrow in losing, and account at last to be given — while balancing it with the notes that God sometimes makes good men rich, that such riches are the fruit of his blessing, and that piety consists very well with prosperity; and warn that places of temptation must be left as soon as possible.

Remark how surprising it is that the Egyptians let the acquired wealth be carried off; set the patriarch against the common case, since moderate wealth hinders many from raising their heads toward heaven while abundance buries men in the earth, and show that he refused the fair pretext of staying where God had blessed him; report two rabbinic accounts of his journeys, of courtesy to former hosts and of pacing suited to the herds; and define calling on the name of the Lord as public profession rather than private prayer.

Note that the property of those times was not flocks only but silver and gold, and pass on the report that part of it was earned by teaching the Egyptians arts and sciences; place the south in Canaan rather than Egypt; and conjecture that the altar was gone because Abram had taken it down himself to keep it from Canaanite pollution, so that he returned to the place of it either to revive the memory of communion or to pay his vows.
Confirm that the word for rich means weighty, and note that the possessions counted include slaves as well as cattle and treasure.

debates: What the word for rich implies about wealth, and whether prosperity consorts with piety.
Whether wealth given by God may be a reason for staying where it was gained.
How long the stay in Egypt lasted, and how the wealth was acquired.
What calling on the name of the Lord means, and what became of the altar.
outliers: Henry alone turns the weight of riches into a catalogue of six burdens.
Calvin alone remarks that the Egyptians might have been expected not to let the wealth leave.
Gill alone sets a three-month chronology beside a twenty-year one and leaves both standing.
Wesley supposes Abram dismantled his own altar to keep the Canaanites from polluting it.
Calvin alone distinguishes invoking God from public profession, and rejects the reading that makes the inhabitants converts.

4.pericope_label: The place of the altar, and the strife that wealth made between the herdsmen

schools.summary: Offer three accounts of the vanished altar — that it fell of itself, that the Canaanites destroyed it, or that Abram took it down to keep it from pollution — and note that the text says he came to the place of the altar and not to the altar; refuse to impute the quarrel either to Abram's moroseness or to his nephew's forwardness, and assign it instead to the design of God, who allays the sweetness of wealth with bitterness lest a servant's mind be enchanted by success; and draw from it a restraint on inordinate desire and a medicine for the troubled rich.

Trace the quarrel to the riches and distinguish two effects, that wealth set the men at a distance because the place was too strait, and set them at variance because riches breed contention among relations — with the observation that every comfort in this world has its cross attending it; and account for the nephew's prosperity by his company, since those who share the obedience of God's people share their comforts.

Give three causes of the separation rather than one, the size of the flocks, the ground already occupied by Canaanite and Perizzite, and an envy between the herdsmen that the text does not state; and note what the flocks supplied, clothing and food and drink, besides the beasts offered in sacrifice.

State the pressure exactly, that the land did not furnish grazing for herds so numerous and that the presence of Canaanite and Perizzite increased the difficulty; and explain the elder man's generosity in yielding the choice by his confident assurance that the Lord would so direct it that the promise would be fulfilled.

debates: What became of the altar Abram had built before going down to Egypt.
Whether the quarrel is to be blamed on either party, or referred to the purpose of God.
What caused the separation besides the size of the flocks.
Why the elder man left the choice of country to the younger.
outliers: Calvin alone puts the question of fault and then sets it aside for the design of God.
Calvin alone measures the loss by saying Abram would sooner have cast away his riches than his nephew.
Clarke alone adds envy between the herdsmen as a cause the narrative does not mention.
Keil alone grounds the magnanimity in a confidence that the promise governed the outcome.
Gill offers three explanations of the altar's disappearance and commits to none of them.

7.pericope_label: The Canaanite in the land, the appeal to brotherhood, and the choice offered to Lot

schools.summary: Read the note about the Canaanite and Perizzite as geography, reconstructing the Perizzites as a townless pastoral people pushed inland by maritime settlers, so that the districts were divided between them and two great clans could find no unoccupied pasture; and describe the country surrendered, the whole circuit of the Jordan watered like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt.

Read the same clause morally, since the quarrel was dangerous, the common enemy being at hand to plunder both if they fell out, and scandalous, the neighbours watching them for the singularity of their religion and ready to improve the quarrel to their reproach; list what the kinship amounted to — one family, one God worshipped alike, one promise, one end — and lay down that where strife is unavoidable in a situation the situation must be changed, no secular advantage counterbalancing the loss of peace.

Report what the herdsmen were likely quarrelling over and set aside a rabbinic account in which the nephew's men justified trespass by his expectation of inheriting; draw from the size of the household an argument for small establishments, since a crowd is commonly turbulent and repose is best had in a small house; warn that when Satan cannot raise enmity between us directly he entangles us in the quarrels of others; explain why the masters are named when only the servants strove; and admit that the appeal to kinship is a lower motive called in because the fear of God is less effectual with us than it should be.

debates: Why the presence of the Canaanite and the Perizzite is mentioned at this point.
What the herdsmen were contending for.
Why Abram speaks of strife between himself and Lot when only their servants were quarrelling.
On what ground the elder man gives up the choice that was his by right.
outliers: Ellicott alone reconstructs the settlement of the country to explain why there was no room.
Wesley alone gives the danger and the scandal of the quarrel as the reason the clause is added.
Gill alone reports the rabbinic story in which the nephew's herdsmen defend trespass by his expectation of inheriting.
Calvin alone turns the episode into an argument for keeping a small household.
Calvin alone admits that the appeal to blood is used because a higher motive is not strong enough in us.

10.pericope_label: Lot lifts up his eyes, chooses the plain of Jordan, and pitches toward Sodom

schools.summary: Note that the nephew had not the ingenuity to return the choice, and take the lifting up of the eyes chiefly of the understanding unless he stood on some eminence; say that he should have contended with his uncle for the palm of modesty and that whoever is intent on his own advantage wants humanity towards others; and refuse the reading that makes the garden of the Lord mean merely excellent, since Moses does not propose a general similitude but says that region was watered, as he had of the first abode of man.

Look for reluctance at the parting and the civility of returning the choice, find neither, and conclude that passion and selfishness make men rude; then trace what the choice cost — captivity, a vexed soul, and at last the mountain he had refused — laying down that sensual choices are sinful choices, that God often gives great plenty to great sinners, and that the righteous man's coming among them was a mercy, since God sends preachers before he sends destroyers.

Make a maxim of it, that a little civility or good breeding is of great importance in the concerns of life; gloss the garden of the Lord in five words as paradise; and repair the awkward clause by re-ordering it after Houbigant, so that before the destruction the land was, as thou goest to Zoar, well watered as paradise was by its four streams and Egypt by the overflowing of the Nile.

Describe the Jordan valley as a geological fault lying below the level of the Mediterranean, once a chain of lakes, now dried by the loss of the forests and receding to leave salt wastes; put the chooser on the high ground between Bethel and Ai and argue from the sightline that the city stood at the north end of the sea; emend Zoar to Zoan on the Syriac; and read the separation as God's own will, the promise renewed afterwards being an inward assurance, since the verb of speaking is unaccompanied by any appearing.

debates: What is meant by lifting up the eyes — sight from a height, or the mind casting about.
How to construe the clause as thou comest unto Zoar, whether by emending the name or by re-ordering the sentence.
Whether the garden of the Lord means Eden specifically or is a Hebrew idiom for anything excellent.
Whether the separation was merely Lot's doing or was according to the will of God.
outliers: Ellicott alone gives the geology of the valley and places the cities at the northern end of the sea.
Ellicott alone emends Zoar to Zoan; Clarke alone repairs the same clause by Houbigant's re-ordering, leaving the name standing.
Calvin alone insists that Eden itself is pointed out rather than a general figure for fertility.
Keil alone infers the inward mode of the renewed promise from the absence of any word of appearing.

13.pericope_label: The wickedness of Sodom, and the promise renewed to Abram after the parting

schools.summary: Set out the fork, that the nephew either did not know what the men of the city were or knew and was tempted anyway, and add the rabbinic reading of the particle as although; raise as a difficulty why they are called wicked before the Lord and not before men, and answer that they were abandoned to execrable crimes whose cry rose to heaven; argue that a fertile country granted to the unworthy gives the wicked no ground of self-congratulation and the godly no reason to envy them; call the word of God the medicine brought to alleviate the pain of the parting; find the design of the separation in the fact that the land was assigned to one man alone; reject the speculation that God spoke through a prophet; take the gift as title now and possession hereafter; and deny that for ever simply denotes perpetuity.

Take the two words to their roots — the one meaning to break in pieces and afflict, so that these men confounded the distinctions between right and wrong, the other to miss the mark, so that a sinner ever aims at happiness and constantly misses it — and make the phrase before the Lord the mark of sinners of no common character; compress the same into three words, impudent daring sinners; suppose the angel of the covenant appeared in open day, since the land was to be viewed and the dust numbered, where the later revelation was plainly at night; and cap for ever at the coming of Christ by lexicon, the word meaning either eternity or a hidden period closing a dispensation.

Make the timing the whole point and give four senses to the phrase after that Lot was separated from him — after the quarrel was over, since calm spirits are best prepared for grace; after the self-denying condescension, God making up in spiritual peace what is lost for neighbourly peace; after the loss of a kinsman's society, communion with God supplying the want of conversation with friends; and after the departure to the plain, lest there be envy, since the one had the paradise but the other had the promise.
Weigh what the parting cost, the relative having shared the exile and being probably regarded as heir in a childless state, so that the promise is made more definite in compensation.

debates: Whether the choice was made in ignorance of the neighbours or in spite of them.
Why the men of the city are called wicked before the Lord rather than before men.
In what manner the word came to Abram — an articulate voice, a visible appearance in daylight, or a prophet's mouth.
How far the term for ever extends.
outliers: Clarke alone works both words back to their roots to define what wickedness and sin are.
Calvin alone turns the fertility of the condemned country into a warning against envying the prosperous wicked.
Henry alone makes the timing of the visit the substance of the passage, drawing four lessons from a single clause.
Ellicott alone reads the promise as consolation for the loss of a presumed heir.

16.pericope_label: The seed as the dust, the command to walk the land, and the altar at Mamre

schools.summary: Call the dust a hyperbolical expression for the multitude of the posterity, in Solomon's days and in the latter day and especially of the spiritual seed; take the command to walk as survey and seisin, adding the Targum's note that possession was made by walking; be interested in the oaks as shade rather than as a shrine, while granting that later superstition may have taken its rise there; but also set aside the subtleties of others, find the force of the promise in the gap between a solitary man and the countless particles of dust, read the circuit of the land as designed to make him perceive himself a stranger and despair of stable possession, treat the verb as a difficulty between pitched and removed, and explain the altar as a public profession of the true God among profane altars, consecrated by the word.

Take the dust the same practical way and point to the multitude under Solomon; make the removing of the tent a lesson in not fixing here but walking through to a better Canaan in the condition of a pilgrim; derive the word for altar from a root meaning to slay, so that sacrifice was offered, and read the building of it as thankfulness for the visit; identify the Amorite and the city of the four; and close the chapter on riches, since happiness has its seat in the mind and earthly goods engender care, anxiety and strife.

Explain why a nomad must change his ground at all, the uplands being rich in spring, burnt up in summer and exposed to winds and rain in winter, and add that the walking now carries the pleasure of knowing his seed will inherit each spot; derive Hebron from alliance, perhaps from the confederacy with the Amorite, and take it for a district as well as a city.

debates: What the comparison to dust is meant to convey, and how a childless man is to receive it.
Why Abram is commanded to walk the length and breadth of the land — to take possession, or to learn that he has none.
Whether the verb at the last verse means pitched or removed.
Why the altar was built, and what the oaks of Mamre were chosen for.
outliers: Gill alone reports the Targum's note that possession was legally made by walking, and alone reports the later veneration of Abram's oak.
Calvin alone reads the circuit of the land as an exercise designed to make Abram feel a stranger rather than an owner.
Ellicott alone explains the necessity behind a nomad's repeated change of ground.
Clarke alone turns the close of the chapter into a verdict on riches.
